As a booking agent, it is your job to secure the best seat for your customers by ensuring they are listening to bands that feature their favorite instruments — and it wouldn't hurt if you seat them next to friends and family! Bebop features area majority via the placement of tiles (reserved seats) and dice (fans). The player who most cleverly outmaneuvers the others on the shared board will get the best rating for their booking agency and thus the most points. [Rating: 1/10] I love knizia boardgames so I was attracted by this one.  Unfortunately this game is confusing and not really playable. Complex scoring game and hard to parse scoring make the whole experience bad  The die drafting and rolling is frustrating and make the whole  experience lack of creative choices more random.  I hoped I could love such game as cascadero or other titles I like but is a bid deception

[Rating: 1/10] Slow and plodding experience—it's not a "long" game, yet it crawls at a snail's pace. Turns are unexciting, formulaic, and constrained. Scoring is incredibly unintuitive and convoluted considering how ostensibly simple the rules are. Interaction between players must be initiated by the players themselves, otherwise you'll each be off doing your own thing and that's more boring yet. Wanted to love this because of the theme, but even that is barely present while playing. Hard pass.

[Rating: 1/10] What a mess. It's sort of Knizia-shaped, but added 500% more icing on top. Claim a seat, roll a die, it feels like the game should be going twice as fast. But why's it so bizzarely complex? Colors, shapes, it's nonsense to even explain what the objective is.  Why is it even called Bebop? It's a weird trend I keep seeing in boardgames, where you play as MIDDLE MANAGERS running things efficiently. Probably to keep all the actual jazz OUT of this. At least Knizia did a game where you play as the band itself.... sorta.  Also I'm baffled why this is called "OG" by everyone. I mean I guess it has th

[Rating: 2/10] This game, while quite obviously wearing its Babylonia and Samurai influences (and trying to straddle a space somewhere between them), is simultaneously simpler yet more opaque than Babylonia, and the scoring in particular is confusing and obtuse, making it an unappealing alternative to Samurai. I cannot imagine a scenario where I would choose to play or recommend Bebop over either of its clear progenitors.

[Rating: 2/10] I hated this. Convoluted rules plus a serious placement game with too much luck. I can handle the color drafting, but that PLUS the die rolling is too much. Why even put dice in this game?

[Rating: 3/10] I just didnt care about what I was doing.  Felt like I was playing a more convoluted version of Babylonia.

[Rating: 3/10] Bebop feels heavily inspired by a few Reiner Knizia games: Samurai, Babylonia, Rebirth.  While it would be a tall order for Bebop to be "better" than any of those games, Bebop manages to feel too similar and mess up the execution so badly.  Ownership depends on coloured tiles, not the vibrantly coloured dice which sit in them.  Some players had difficulty with this throughout the entire game.  Bebop really feels like a game that is all flash and no substance.  This was a pretty tough slog for the whole table.  The decision space is massive and becomes strictly smaller with each turn. [Rating: 4/10] An anti-Knizia abstract - overly complex with bloated scoring options. I’m not into abstracts in general unless they are lean and can be explained in less than 10 minutes. This one couldn’t. The dice were particularly painful visually - although they are made nicely.

[Rating: 4/10] its functional? but didnt really find it fun.          dont think id play it over other knizian tile layers.

[Rating: 4/10] Maybe with subsequent plays, the fun will appear, but it did not show itself in the first play.  The game is slow as it takes two turns to do what would be one turn in other tile layers.  The scoring is confused and rewards boring play.  I would try it again, but it might be difficult to find a table that is both willing to play this and has already played it.

[Rating: 4/10] Bebop is a tile placement game that also makes use of dice. On a turn you'll either claim a hex space that on a later turn you can place a die on or use your turn to place a die onto a spot you've calimed. The aim is to create families of colors to score points, but the families also help scoring stages that are on the board. Each stage wants certain types of musical instruments surrounding it with these instruments being included if they are also in the same color family of any die touching that stage. [Rating: 4.5/10] Why I culled it (Jun. 2026): Really disappointing, given the comparisons to games like Babylonia and Samurai. First and foremost, colorblindness made the game practically unplayable for me. Colors are way too similar and have to be read at a distance on small, engraved dice. Scoring is convoluted and poorly explained in the rules. We were still trying to figure it out at game end.   The game itself just isn't good, either. [Rating: 4.5/10] Fun theme (but it could've been anything really) and cool artwork that unfortunately doesn't translate very well to the game itself. I've played a few games on BGA and couldn't really get used to the boards. They look busy and I miss the option to cover the parts that aren't used at lower player count, which is distracting. The color choice for tiles and dice is also questionable as some colors are very similar, which makes it even harder to have a good overview of what's going on on the board (and I'm not even color blind).  I feel like it's a fairly simple game that's been overly convoluted 

[Rating: 5/10] Rules are a bit inelegant from the usual fare you get from these type of old school German abstracts, but the gameplay is good and interesting enough. Nothing special, alas, that would warrant a higher rating than this

[Rating: 5/10] I don't think so much randomness was necessary for a tile-laying game. Board is very annoying to parse. I didn't absolutely hate it and it is probably better on further play but my initial impressions are just that I'd much rather play Babylonia.

[Rating: 5/10] A strategic area controlling-ish game where players are battles to take control of markers based on the icons in each region, from 1 to 3 icons. Each region is resolved once all non star spaces next to region is filled with a dice, then for each icon in that region, count of all icons connected by the same color matching that region. These icons are going to be used for scoring at the end of the game based on the longest region of that color and contains the most of all the icons gets to score.
